newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU insists its view on Boeing merger not political.
newsitem.headline: EU insists its view on Boeing merger not political.

text.p: The European Commission strongly rejected on Thursday any suggestions that plans to ban the Boeing /McDonnell Douglas merger are politically motivated, insisting its analysis is based on hard facts and figures.
But its statements are unlikely to convince angry U.S. lawmakers who believe the EU executive is simply acting on behalf of Airbus Industrie, the four-nation European aircraft consortium.

In contrast to the Commission, which feels the merger in its present form would harm competition on the aircraft market, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) earlier this month approved the deal without conditions.
These conflicting views of the same deal could create the impression that Brussels and Washington are trying to promote the interests of their own aerospace industries.
"People are sensing that this is all politically motivated, that the EU is protecting its champion and the United States is pretecting its champion," said a competition lawyer.
"I think there is a very strong element of defending a flagship industry," added another competition expert in Brussels.

On Wednesday, the EU's advisory committee on competition firmly backed the Commission's view that concessions offered by Boeing to win approval for the planned $14 billion deal were not enough to address EU antitrust concerns.

Members of the U.S. Congress were quick to denounce the EU stance as outrageous and ludicrous, and the Senate unanimously approved a measure condemning the EU for its expected rejection of the merger.
Republican Senator Slade Gorton, from Boeing's home state of Washington, made no secret of why he believes the Commission is against the merger to create the world's largest aerospace firm.

"The sole true reason for the European Commission's criticism and imminent disapproval of the merger is to gain an unfair competitive advantage for Airbus, a government-owned aircraft manufacturer," he said in a statement.
The EU executive was quick to react to this and a call by a White House spokesman that the merger be examined solely on the basis of EU antitrust law.
"We are looking at the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger according to very objective criteria...there are no political considerations," Commission President Jacques Santer told a news conference.
However, contrasting regulatory views have raised questions about how two competition authorities could reach opposite conclusions when analysing the impact on competition of the same merger.

"It is curious that a merger that takes place in the United States is seen as creating a dominant position in Europe but is not thought by U.S. authorities to cause a serious competition problem in the United States," one competition lawyer said.

He and other competition policy experts say politics could be a factor in views of the case on both sides of the Atlantic. But they also stress that the Commission and the FTC could genuinely interpret the same facts differently.

Last year, for example, the FTC approved the merger between Swiss drug companies Sandoz and Ciba Geigy only after ordering a $780 million divestiture, while the Brussels-based executive imposed smaller conditions.

In the Boeing/McDonnell case, while the FTC argues that McDonnell Douglas no longer is a "meaningful competitive force" in the commercial aircraft market, the EU executive insists that the firm adds to Boeing's dominant position.

"I'm not naive, so I think that there are some non-competition aspects involved in this," said one lawyer. "It is quite clear that the reason why the Commission has come to a different conclusion is because it has listened more to Airbus while on the FTC side they may have listened more to Boeing."
